messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan, a 29-year-old salesperson, had always found comfort in the great outdoors. Growing up in a small town nestled amidst rolling hills and lush forests, he often spent his weekends hiking, camping, and simply enjoying nature. However, everything changed one fateful afternoon when a sudden and catastrophic tornado swept through his town, leaving destruction in its wake. Ethan was at home when he first heard the deafening roar; he rushed to the window just in time to see the sky darkening ominously. The terror of that moment was etched into his memory as he dove for cover, feeling the vibrations of the earth shake beneath him as the storm ripped through his community. 

In the months that followed, Ethan began to notice how certain physical locations triggered intense feelings of vulnerability. Visiting a park where trees had been uprooted and homes reduced to rubble filled him with dread. Even the gentle rustling of leaves would trigger flashbacks, transporting him back to the moment he felt utterly powerless. Each time he found himself in nature, whether on a hike or simply sitting outside, he was overwhelmed by a visceral terror, as if the disaster were happening all over again. These experiences were compounded by feelings of emotional vulnerability; Ethan had come to believe he could no longer trust his own ability to navigate the world safely.

As these triggers intensified, Ethan's memories of that day became fragmented and distorted. He would often feel the overwhelming emotional intensity of the tornado without a clear recollection of the specifics. It was as though the horror of the event was locked away in a haze, and he could only grasp at it, leading to a deep sense of frustration and helplessness. He struggled with gaps in his memory, unable to piece together all the terrifying details of the day. When he did manage to recall snippets, the raw terror he felt at that time washed over him anew, plunging him into a state of panic that kept him on high alert.

Ethan's negative appraisals of himself and his life began to take root as well. He felt a profound sense of identity loss, as if the person he once was had been swallowed by the catastrophe. Nothing seemed meaningful anymore; he often found himself questioning the purpose of his life and feeling disconnected from those around him. This mistrust seeped into his relationships, leading him to believe he couldn't rely on others for support. He felt isolated, convinced that no one could truly understand the depths of his trauma. More than ever, he felt that he was on his own in a world that felt dangerous and unpredictable.

These negative beliefs only sharpened his sense of threat. The fear of having his autonomy taken away again loomed large in his mind, compelling him to remain hypervigilant. Each night, he woke abruptly, checking his surroundings to ensure his safety, convinced that danger could strike at any moment. This constant state of alertness created a cycle where his memories of the tornado would trigger feelings of vulnerability, while his negative self-appraisals reinforced his belief that he was unworthy of help or connection. 

As time went on, Ethan's world shrank. He avoided places that reminded him of the disaster, sacrificing his love for nature in favor of the perceived safety of his home. Yet, the walls of his apartment felt like a prison, and the isolation deepened his despair. He felt trapped in a cycle where every attempt to escape his memories only seemed to solidify them further, and he feared he would never regain the joy he once found in life.

Finally, after months of struggling in silence, Ethan found himself sitting in a therapist's office, driven by the desperate hope that he might reclaim a sense of normalcy. He was terrified at the prospect of reliving the trauma through therapy but knew he could no longer bear the weight of his isolation and fear. What he hoped for most was to rediscover not only the world outside but also the person he used to be—a person who could find peace in the beauty of nature without the shadow of terror looming over him.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that triggers influence Ethan's memories of the tornado.
The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals influence Ethan's sense of threat.

The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals influence the triggers Ethan experiences.
